newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Biting farm-tax bullet poses challenge to Bhutto.
newsitem.headline: Biting farm-tax bullet poses challenge to Bhutto.

text.p: Pakistani markets favour IMF-inspired proposals to impose a farm-income tax, but collecting it from wealthy landlords may prove tough for Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, analysts said on Monday.
Newspapers reported that provincial chief ministers agreed at a meeting with Bhutto and President Farooq Leghari on Sunday to implement the tax, a prerogative of provincial governments.

"Benazir Bhutto has a chance to create history," Kalim Aziz, senior analyst at ING Baring Securities, told Reuters, adding that a government success in pushing agricultural income tax through would boost the depressed Karachi stock market.
The 100-share index closed up 9.16 points or 0.67 percent at 1,383.79 on Monday, helped by reports of the tax plan.
Pakistani officials left for Washington on Sunday to discuss a rescue package with the International Monetary Fund, widely believed to include an agricultural income tax.
"This tax should go as a right signal for the IMF and we believe they will agree to release the remaining part of its $600 million standby loan," Aziz said.
The IMF has held up disbursements of the standby loan because of doubts about Pakistan's implementation of agreed reforms and confusion over the 1996/97 (July-June) budget.
It cannot disburse the delayed payments until a mission has visited Pakistan and completed a review of the economy.

Analysts say the largely untapped pool of revenue from farm income could convince the IMF to resume disbursements, but some warned that the tax could be hard to collect, given the political clout of Pakistan's powerful landlords.
Three provinces passed legislation in June 1994 to introduce agricultural income tax, but provincial government officials say resistance from big landowners has kept receipts negligible.
Punjab province has not even introduced the tax due to opposition from the rich landowners who dominate the provincial assembly.

"If collection is low, the tax would be of no consequence," said the treasury head of a foreign bank, who declined to be identified. The IMF would be unimpressed if the government projected that it would raise only a few billion rupees, he said.
"If the total agriculture income is estimated at 550 billion rupees ($14.84 billion), the tax should recover at least 27.5 billion rupees, which is five percent of the total," he said.
Analyst Nauman Sheikh of KASB & Co, a brokerage house, said a comprehensive tax on agricultural income should net more than 10 billion rupees, but he anticipated low receipts at first.
"We think the first-year collection would be anywhere from two billion to ten billion rupees," Sheikh said.
Aziz said the tax should be relatively easy to administer because agriculture was the best-documented economic sector.
"People have been declaring their agricultural income quite honestly to benefit from the exemptions," he said, adding that the government could achieve whatever target it decides to set.

Aziz said Pakistan's gross domestic product was 2,850 billion rupees in fiscal 1995/96 (July-June). "With agriculture accounting for 24 percent of GDP, we should have a taxable income of 70 billion rupees," he said.
